paras: The attempted lynching of James Derossett was a failed mob attempt in late March 1888 to take Derossett, who was charged with killing a man named Smith near Dayton, Tennessee, from the Dayton jail and hang him. The sheriff removed the prisoner before the mob reached him, and no injury to Derossett was reported. The episode reached readers in several Southern states through short telegraphic briefs that disagreed on the dead man's first name and on where Derossett was taken.

According to a Chattanooga special dispatch to the Memphis Appeal, Derossett and a companion named Gazaway Smith "got into a difficulty" near Dayton, and Derossett was said to have struck Smith on the head with a rock, crushing his skull and killing him. The dispatch added that he threw the body into a creek swollen by recent rains and left. Condensed versions of the report dated the killing "on the 27th."

Deputy Marshal Hill and the town marshal of Dayton arrested Derossett, but he broke away before he was taken to town and ran to the woods while the officers fired fifteen pistol shots at him, none of which stopped him. The dispatch reported that the people were "greatly excited" and that a posse was pursuing him that night.

A Chattanooga dispatch printed in the Weekly Courier-Journal stated that Derossett, there called James DeRosset, was captured at Spring City and locked up in the Dayton jail. The same dispatch said that a mob went to the jail at night to take him out and hang him, but the sheriff slipped the prisoner out the back way and took him to Graysville, "thereby preventing a lynching." A later brief gave a different destination, stating that he was taken to Chattanooga and locked up in jail there to prevent his lynching, and that "a mob intended to hang him at Dayton." Neither account gives the size of the mob or names any of its members.
No report of arrests of mob members, of an indictment, or of a trial of Derossett was found in the coverage.

The story first appeared as a special dispatch to the Memphis Appeal under the headlines "A Murder at Dayton" and "The Criminal Succeeds in Running the Gauntlet—Much Excitement." That dispatch called Derossett "the murderer" and described him as "desperate from his terrible crime," treating the accusation as settled before any trial. On March 31 a condensed version ran among the "Late News Items" of the Huntsville Gazette and the "Condensed Telegrams" of the Osceola Times in Arkansas.

The jail attempt reached Kentucky readers on April 2, when the Weekly Courier-Journal printed it under the headline "A Lynching Party Failed." A shorter account in the syndicated "Southern Gleanings" column ran in the Bolivar Bulletin on April 6 and in the Huntsville Gazette and the Grenada Sentinel on April 7. None of the reports stated the race of Derossett or of Smith, and none commented on the mob beyond noting that a lynching had been prevented.

The reports disagree on the name of the dead man: the first dispatch and its condensation called him Gazaway Smith, while the later accounts called him Ras Smith. They also differ on where Derossett was taken, Graysville according to the Courier-Journal dispatch and Chattanooga according to the "Southern Gleanings" brief; the coverage does not show whether he was moved to both places. The dates are inconsistent as printed: the Memphis Appeal dispatch is datelined March 29 in an issue dated March 27, the condensed brief dates the killing to the 27th, and the Courier-Journal dispatch, datelined "March 20," places it on a Tuesday.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of James Derossett
bases: A mob went to the Dayton jail to take out and hang Derossett, an accused murderer, and was foiled when the sheriff removed him (A4, A5).
No one was killed: the sheriff slipped Derossett out of the jail before the mob could hang him (A4, A5); the mob acted without authority on a murder accusation, but its size is not given.

Two differently worded dispatches (A4 and the Southern Gleanings brief A5) agree that a mob intended to hang Derossett and that he was removed from Dayton to prevent it, though they name different destinations.

accounts.label: Chattanooga special dispatch (first report)
accounts.gist: Derossett killed Gazaway Smith with a rock after a difficulty, escaped two officers under fifteen shots, and was pursued by a posse amid excitement.

accounts.label: Chattanooga dispatch, Courier-Journal
accounts.gist: DeRosset, captured at Spring City and jailed at Dayton, was taken out the back way to Graysville by the sheriff when a mob came to hang him.

accounts.label: Southern Gleanings brief
accounts.gist: Derossett, charged with murdering Ras Smith, was taken to Chattanooga jail to prevent lynching; a mob intended to hang him at Dayton.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal's 'A Murder at Dayton' treated Derossett's guilt as fact ('the murderer', 'desperate from his terrible crime') and stressed local excitement.
'A Lynching Party Failed' and the Southern Gleanings brief reported the foiled mob flatly, without comment on the mob.

conflicts.note: Neither version is clearly better; A1 is the earliest and most detailed, A4/A5 are later.
Possibly successive moves; the coverage does not say.
